claim: A novel doxycycline (DOX)-inducible CRISPR gene activation system (iCRISPRa) was developed to drive the expression of multiple endogenous transcription factors important for in vitro cell fate and differentiation of iPSCs to haematopoietic progenitor cells.
source: We then developed a novel doxycycline (DOX)-inducible CRISPR gene activation system to assess the role of the genes that were expressed at a lower level within in vitro-derived cells compared to their in vivo counterparts.
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and application of the iCRISPRa system with experimental validation.

claim: Nine candidate transcription factors (RUNX1T1, NR4A1, GATA2, SMAD7, ZNF124, SOX6, ZNF33A, NFAT5, and TFDP2) were predicted to be involved in blood cell emergence during development.
source: This strategy identified nine target transcription factors RUNX1T1, NR4A1, GATA2, SMAD7, ZNF124, SOX6, ZNF33A, NFAT5, and TFDP2 (Figure 1C), whose expression was detected across other AGM datasets in the haemogenic endothelium (Calvanese et al., 2022; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The genes were identified through comparative transcriptomic analysis and validated in published datasets.

claim: iCRISPRa activation of endogenous transcription factors resulted in a significant expansion of arterial-fated endothelial cells expressing high levels of IGFBP2.
source: iCRISPRa activation of these endogenous TFs resulted in a significant expansion of arterial-fated endothelial cells expressing high levels of IGFBP2
evidence: The manuscript presents scRNAseq data and flow cytometry showing expansion of arterial cells and IGFBP2 expression.

claim: IGFBP2 is involved in the remodelling of metabolic activity during in vitro endothelial to haematopoietic transition.
source: our analysis indicated that IGFBP2 is involved in the remodelling of metabolic activity during in vitro endothelial to haematopoietic transition.
evidence: The manuscript provides metabolic profiling data showing changes in oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis.

claim: HSPCs are generated by a subset of endothelial cells known as haemogenic endothelium during development.
source: During development, HSPCs are generated by a subset of endothelial cells, known as haemogenic endothelium (Jaffredo et al., 1998; Zovein et al., 2008; Bertrand et al., 2010; Boisset et al., 2010), via the endothelial to haematopoietic transition (EHT) Ottersbach, 2019.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: During the EHT, endothelial cells undergo profound transcriptional remodelling whereby the expression of endothelial genes is gradually downregulated, and the transcription of the haematopoietic program is initiated.
source: During the EHT, endothelial cells undergo profound transcriptional remodelling whereby the expression of endothelial genes is gradually downregulated, and the transcription of the haematopoietic program is initiated (Swiers et al., 2013) while the cells round up and eventually detach to enter the circulation (Kissa and Herbomel, 2010; Eilken et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The comparison of in vitro-derived haemogenic endothelium to in vivo HSC-primed human haemogenic endothelium identified transcription factors expressed at lower levels in vitro.
source: To explore the molecular control on the development of the haematopoietic system and to address the differences with the in vitro differentiation of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), we compared our single-cell transcriptomics analysis of in vitro-derived haemogenic endothelium and early progenitors (Fidanza et al., 2020) to that of the in vivo HSC-primed human haemogenic endothelium (Zeng et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript describes the comparative analysis with specific datasets cited.

claim: The iSAM system can induce gene expression that predictably translates into increased protein expression.
source: Altogether, these results show that the iSAM system is able to induce gene expression that predictably translates into an increased protein expression and thus provides a platform to steer phenotypical changes in cell identity.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing correlation between gene activation and protein expression.

claim: The addition of a capture sequence to the gRNA backbone enabled their detection within the scRNAseq pipeline without altering the level of endogenous gene activation.
source: We compared the activation level achieved with the new 2.1 gRNA to that of the original 2.0 backbone using various gRNAs targeting RUNX1C (Figure 2F). These results convincingly demonstrated that the addition of the capture sequence in the gRNA 2.1 does not alter the level of endogenous gene activation that could be achieved (Figure 2G).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data comparing gRNA 2.0 and 2.1 performance.

claim: DOX treatment resulted in an average 3.33±0.73-fold increase of CD34+DLL4+ immunophenotypic arterial cells in iSAM-AGM cells.
source: Although DOX treatment resulted in an average 1.63±0.13-fold increase of CD34+DLL4+ cells in the control iSAM_NT sample (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), the increase observed in the iSAM-AGM cells was significantly greater, with an expansion of 3.33±0.73-fold increase of CD34+DLL4+ immunophenotypic arterial cells identified by flow cytometry (Figure 3F).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative flow cytometry data.

claim: Activation of target transcription factors using the CRISPR strategy resulted in an increased number of CFU-E and CFU-GM and a reduction of CFU-M in iSAM-AGM samples cultured in the presence of DOX.
source: We detected an increased number of CFU-E (colony-forming unit erythroid) and CFU-GM (colony-forming unit granulocyte/macrophage) and a reduction of CFU-M (colony-forming unit macrophage) in iSAM-AGM samples cultured in the presence of DOX compared to the absence of DOX but no significant effect of DOX in SAM_NT samples (Figure 3G).
evidence: The manuscript presents colony-forming unit assay data.

claim: IGFBP2 was the most upregulated gene in arterial cells upon activation of the target genes.
source: To better understand the molecular mechanism behind the increased progenitor development, we compared the expression profile of the arterial cells between the different activation libraries, and we obtained a list of genes upregulated upon activation of the targets (Supplementary file 1). The most upregulated gene, IGFBP2, was expressed at significantly higher levels in the iSAM_AGM library in the presence of DOX compared to the others (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents scRNAseq data showing differential gene expression.

claim: RUNX1T1-specific gRNAs were significantly enriched in arterial cells from the iSAM_AGM treated with DOX.
source: We then compared the gRNA distribution in these arterial cells from the iSAM_AGM treated with DOX to that of arterial cells without activation. We observed a significant enrichment of the RUNX1T1-specific gRNAs (Supplementary file 1), indicating that the increased IGFBP2 expression could be downstream of RUNX1T1 activation.
evidence: The manuscript presents gRNA distribution analysis from scRNAseq data.

claim: The increased IGFBP2 expression could be downstream of RUNX1T1 activation.
source: We observed a significant enrichment of the RUNX1T1-specific gRNAs (Supplementary file 1), indicating that the increased IGFBP2 expression could be downstream of RUNX1T1 activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of RUNX1T1 gRNAs in cells with high IGFBP2 expression.

claim: Cells treated with IGFBP2 showed a significant increase in the total number of haematopoietic CFU colonies compared to cells in control cultures.
source: Cells treated with IGFBP2 showed a significant increase in the total number of haematopoietic CFU colonies compared to cells in control cultures.
evidence: The manuscript presents colony-forming unit assay data comparing IGFBP2-treated and control cells.

claim: IGFBP2 treatment did not affect the production of arterial cells themselves.
source: To assess whether IGFBP2 also affected the production of arterial cells themselves, we analysed the proportion of DLL4+ cells, but no difference was detected in the presence of IGFBP2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing no change in DLL4+ cells.

claim: The mechanism of action of IGFBP2 is different from that mediated by the gene activation that led to an expansion of the arterial population.
source: This implies that the mechanism of action of IGFBP2 is different from that mediated by the gene activation that led to an expansion of the arterial population.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that IGFBP2 increases progenitors without increasing arterial cells.

claim: CD34+DLL4+ and CD34+DLL4- cells showed different capacity to generate suspension cells when plated on OP9.
source: CD34+DLL4+ and CD34+DLL4- plated on OP9 showed different capacity to generate suspension cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), in line with the colonies' formation results showing that the DLL4- contains the largest progenitor activity.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from sorted cell populations.

claim: IGFBP2 treatment resulted in a significant expansion of the CD34+ and CD43+ cell populations.
source: Our results showed a significant expansion of the CD34+ and CD43+ cell populations, further supporting our hypothesis (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing expansion of these populations.

claim: IGFBP2 is highly expressed within the AGM niche by stromal and epithelial cells and, most importantly, highest in endothelial cells.
source: IGFBP2 is highly expressed within the AGM niche by stromal and epithelial cells and, most importantly, highest in endothelial cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript presents analysis of published in vivo scRNAseq data from human AGM.

claim: IGFBP2 addition results in increased haematopoietic blood production in vitro.
source: Together these data show that IGFBP2 addition results in increased haematopoietic blood production in vitro and that the endothelial compartment is the most likely source of IGFBP2 both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: The manuscript presents multiple lines of experimental evidence supporting this conclusion.

claim: The endothelial compartment is the most likely source of IGFBP2 both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Together these data show that IGFBP2 addition results in increased haematopoietic blood production in vitro and that the endothelial compartment is the most likely source of IGFBP2 both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from expression analysis in both in vitro and in vivo datasets.

claim: IGFBP2 induced a change in the transcriptome specifically on day 13 of differentiation.
source: Our time course transcriptomic analyses showed that IGFBP2 induced a change in the transcriptome, specifically on day 13 (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript presents time course scRNAseq data.

claim: A cluster of endothelial cells enriched for genes associated with the KEGG pathway of growth factor binding was detected almost exclusively at day 13.
source: A cluster of endothelial cells enriched for genes associated with the KEGG pathway of growth factor binding was detected almost exclusively at day 13 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F)
evidence: The manuscript presents scRNAseq clustering and pathway analysis.

claim: The endothelial cell cluster showed expression of GJA4 across the cells, indicating their broad arterial identity, with a specific reduction of DLL4 expression level concomitantly to an upregulation of RUNX1 in the region of the cluster induced by IGFBP2.
source: Interestingly, this cluster showed expression of GJA4 across the cells, indicating their broad arterial identity, with a specific reduction of DLL4 expression level concomitantly to an upregulation of RUNX1 in the region of the cluster induced by IGFBP2 (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript presents gene expression analysis from scRNAseq data.

claim: IGFBP2 supports arterial cells in the acquisition of haemogenic capacity.
source: This suggests that IGFBP2 supports arterial cells in the acquisition of haemogenic capacity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of increased haemogenic markers in arterial cells treated with IGFBP2.

claim: The genes that were upregulated by IGFBP2 were highly enriched in the oxidative phosphorylation term according to KEGG enrichment analysis.
source: We compared the transcriptome of cells at day 13 in the presence and absence of IGFBP2 and, using KEGG enrichment analysis, we observed that the genes that were upregulated by IGFBP2 were highly enriched in the oxidative phosphorylation term (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: The manuscript presents KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes.

claim: IGFBP2-treated cells showed a reduction in glycolytic-derived ATP, which translates to a higher contribution of mitochondria metabolism.
source: We detected a reduction in glycolytic-derived ATP (Figure 5E and F), which translates to a higher contribution of mitochondria metabolism for IGFBP2-treated cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: The manuscript presents ATP production rate measurements using Seahorse technology.

claim: A general downregulation of the glycolytic enzymes and its checkpoints was observed in IGFBP2-treated cells at day 13 compared to the control on the same day.
source: We observed a general downregulation of the glycolytic enzymes and its checkpoints, with the exception of PFKM and SLC16A1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B), which were expressed at lower levels in the IGFBP2-treated cells at day 13 compared to the control on the same day.
evidence: The manuscript presents gene expression analysis from scRNAseq data.

claim: The IGFBP2-induced remodelling of the endothelial cells' transcriptome happens exclusively on day 13.
source: These differences were not observed on day 10 cells, which is consistent with our previous observations that the IGFBP2-induced remodelling of the endothelial cells' transcriptome happens exclusively on day 13.
evidence: This is inferred from the time course analysis showing differences only at day 13.

claim: No differences in the cell cycle distribution of haematopoietic progenitors were observed with IGFBP2 treatment.
source: To assess whether the higher clonogenic potential and effect on the bioenergetic profile of the cells treated with IGFBP2 was the result of an increase in proliferation, we analysed the cell cycle profile of suspension haematopoietic cells obtained from the OP9 cocultured in the presence of IGFBP2. No differences in the cell cycle distribution of haematopoietic progenitors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) was observed, indicating that the detected increase in haematopoietic progenitors is not likely to be a consequence of their increased cycling.
evidence: The manuscript presents cell cycle analysis data.

claim: The effect of IGFBP2 occurs prior to, or during the emergence of haematopoietic progenitors via the EHT process.
source: We, therefore, concluded the effect of IGBP2 occurs prior to, or during their emergence via the EHT process.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that IGFBP2 does not affect cell cycle but increases progenitors.

claim: The activation of nine target transcription factors leads to the expansion of arterial cells and, consequently, to an increase in progenitor activity.
source: In summary, our results show that the activation of the nine target transcription factors, expressed at higher levels in vivo within the arterial cells in the AGM region, leads to the expansion of the arterial cells and, consequently, to an increase in progenitor activity (Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript presents multiple lines of experimental evidence supporting this conclusion.

claim: The addition of IGFBP2 to the differentiation culture induced the upregulation of RUNX1 and OxPhos genes and accelerated the metabolic dependency on OXPHOS in association with improved progenitor activity.
source: The addition of IGFBP2 to the differentiation culture induced the upregulation of RUNX1 and OxPhos genes and accelerated the metabolic dependency on OXPHOS in association with improved progenitor activity (Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript presents multiple lines of experimental evidence supporting this conclusion.

claim: Some of the identified transcription factors had been previously associated with blood cell development, including GATA2, SMAD7, NR4A1, SOX6, and RUNX1T1.
source: Some of these had been associated with blood cell development, including GATA2 (Castaño et al., 2019; de Pater et al., 2013; Ling et al., 2004), SMAD7 (McGarvey et al., 2017), NR4A1 (McGarvey et al., 2017), SOX6 (McGrath et al., 2011), and RUNX1T1 (Zeng et al., 2019; Calvanese et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ZNF124, ZNF33A, NFAT5, and TFDP2 had not been previously associated with haematopoiesis.
source: Other genes such as ZNF124, ZNF33A, NFAT5, and TFDP2 had not been previously associated with haematopoiesis and could provide early evidence of their possible role in haematopoiesis that will require further studies.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding requiring further investigation.

claim: RUNX1T1 is associated with the leukemic fusion protein, AML1/ETO, resulting from the t(8;21) chromosomal translocation.
source: We were particularly interested in RUNX1T1 (also known as ETO) which is associated with the leukemic fusion protein, AML1/ETO, resulting from the t(8;21) chromosomal translocation (Rejeski et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: RUNX1T1 expression has been recently detected in transcriptomic analyses of the human AGM region.
source: Furthermore, RUNX1T1 expression has been recently detected in transcriptomic analyses of the human AGM region (Zeng et al., 2019; Calvanese et al., 2022), but its precise role during the ontogeny of the blood system has not been elucidated.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: IGFBP2 KO mice show increased expression of cell cycle inhibitors and HSC apoptosis, implicating IGFBP2 as a modulator of HSCs cell cycle and survival.
source: IGFBP2 KO mice show increased expression of cell cycle inhibitors and HSC apoptosis, implicating IGFBP2 as a modulator of HSCs cell cycle and survival (Huynh et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: IGFBP2 was reported as being highly expressed in the human AGM region at CS14 when HSCs are emerging.
source: More recently IGFBP2 was reported as being highly expressed in the human AGM region at CS14 when HSCs are emerging (Calvanese et al., 2022), supporting a possible role during developmental haematopoiesis but the precise molecular process was unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: RUNX1T1 lacks a DNA binding domain.
source: Because RUNX1T1 lacks a DNA binding domain, its direct involvement in the regulation of IGFBP2 expression, or in the development of the haematopoietic system in general, must require association with other cofactors that are yet to be identified.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the protein structure.

claim: The direct involvement of RUNX1T1 in the regulation of IGFBP2 expression must require association with other cofactors that are yet to be identified.
source: Because RUNX1T1 lacks a DNA binding domain, its direct involvement in the regulation of IGFBP2 expression, or in the development of the haematopoietic system in general, must require association with other cofactors that are yet to be identified.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of DNA binding domain in RUNX1T1.

claim: The supportive role of the endothelial niche in the development of HSCs has been studied in vivo.
source: The supportive role of the endothelial niche in the development of HSCs has been studied in vivo (Crosse et al., 2020; Hadland et al., 2022; Hadland et al., 2015) and exploited in vitro to support HSCs emergence (Hadland et al., 2022; Sandler et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The switch between glycolytic to mitochondrial metabolism has been shown to be essential for the EHT in definitive haematopoiesis.
source: The switch between glycolytic to mitochondrial metabolism has been shown to be essential for the EHT in definitive haematopoiesis (Oburoglu et al., 2022; Azzoni et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The metabolic switch is induced in vivo by mechanical cues downstream of the establishment of circulation, and it is required for functional HSCs development.
source: This switch is induced in vivo by mechanical cues downstream of the establishment of circulation, and it is required for functional HSCs development (Azzoni et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In vitro, the metabolic switch is driven by pyruvate mitochondrial catabolism, leading to definitive EHT as opposed to primitive.
source: while in vitro, the switch is driven by pyruvate mitochondrial catabolism, leading to definitive EHT as opposed to primitive (Oburoglu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Combining CRISPR-mediated activation of target genes with single-cell transcriptomic analysis in differentiating hPSCs can be a powerful approach to alter cell fate.
source: This study demonstrates that combining CRISPR-mediated activation of target genes with single-cell transcriptomic analysis in differentiating hPSCs can be a powerful approach to alter cell fate, providing a tool for gene function studies during human development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The fine epigenetic manipulation of the transcription can be readily applied to any cell lineage simply by adding specific gRNAs.
source: The fine epigenetic manipulation of the transcription can be readily applied to any cell lineage simply by adding specific gRNAs and it will be instrumental in exploring other developmental processes that can be, at least partially, mimicked in vitro with hiPSCs.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader applicability of the method.

claim: Some limitations remain in applying CRISPR-mediated gene activation strategies in long differentiation protocols due to the challenge of detecting high copy numbers of the gRNAs.
source: Some limitations remain in applying CRISPR-mediated gene activation strategies in long differentiation protocols due to the challenge of detecting high copy numbers of the gRNAs, limiting the possibility of providing the fine statistical correlation needed to predict downstream target genes.
evidence: This is a discussion of limitations observed in the study.

claim: The iSAM system activated all the target genes except for ZFN124.
source: Following data filtering, we selected cells in which the gRNAs expression was detected and showed that our approach activated all the target genes, except for ZFN124.
evidence: The manuscript presents scRNAseq data showing gene expression levels.

claim: A higher level of expression of RUNX1T1, NR4A1, GATA2, SMAD7, SOX6, ZNF33A, NFAT5, TFDP2 was observed following DOX treatment of iSAM_AGM cells compared to the iSAM_NT cells.
source: A higher level of expression of RUNX1T1, NR4A1, GATA2, SMAD7, SOX6, ZNF33A, NFAT5, TFDP2 was observed following DOX treatment of cells of iSAM_AGM cells compared to the iSAM_NT cells (Figure 3A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: The manuscript presents scRNAseq data showing differential gene expression.

claim: All the clusters expressed pan-endothelial markers such as PECAM1 and CDH5, coding for CD31 and VECAD, respectively, which get progressively downregulated in EHT_1 and EHT_2.
source: All the clusters expressed pan-endothelial markers such as PECAM1 and CDH5, coding for CD31 and VECAD, respectively, which get progressively downregulated in EHT_1 and EHT_2, as expected for cells undergoing the EHT process.
evidence: The manuscript presents scRNAseq data showing marker expression patterns.

claim: The arterial cluster was significantly overrepresented in the DOX-induced iSAM-AGM compared to the iSAM_NT cells.
source: To assess the effect of the activation on cell identity, we analysed the proportion of the cell clusters between the libraries and detected a significant expansion of the arterial cluster in the DOX-induced iSAM-AGM compared to the iSAM_NT cells (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and I).
evidence: The manuscript presents scRNAseq clustering analysis showing cluster proportions.

claim: The AAVS1 locus has been reported to be a 'safe harbour' site that is resistant to epigenetic silencing.
source: The AAVS1 locus has been reported to be a 'safe harbour' site that is resistant to epigenetic silencing and indeed, we had previously demonstrated that transgenes inserted into the AAVS1 locus under the control of the constitutively active CAG promoter were efficiently expressed both in undifferentiated and in differentiated iPSCs (Yang et al., 2017; Lopez-Yrigoyen et al., 2019; Lopez-Yrigoyen et al., 2018; May et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature including the authors' own work.

claim: After the iSAM line had been established and cultured under self-renewal conditions, a dramatic reduction in the number of mCherry+ cells in undifferentiated iSAM iPSCs upon DOX induction was noted.
source: However, after the iSAM line had been established and cultured under self-renewal conditions, we noted a dramatic reduction in the number of mCherry+ cells in undifferentiated iSAM iPSCs upon DOX induction.
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing reduced mCherry expression.

claim: The reduction in mCherry+ cells was predicted to be due to transgene silencing of the rTTA DOX-inducible cassette.
source: We predicted this to be due to transgene silencing of the rTTA DOX-inducible cassette (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of reduced expression over time in culture.

claim: Sodium butyrate treatment had no adverse effect on iPSC maintenance.
source: To overcome this problem, we treated the iSAM iPSC line with an inhibitor of histone deacetylases (HDACs), sodium butyrate (SB), reported to have no adverse effect on iPSC maintenance (Kang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014) and we also confirmed that the treatment with SB had no effect on viability and cell proliferation in our culture conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and confirmed by experimental data.

claim: A short 48 hr treatment with sodium butyrate significantly increased the number of mCherry+ cells upon DOX induction, proportional to the SB concentration.
source: A short 48 hr treatment significantly increased the number of mCherry+ cells upon DOX induction, proportional to the SB concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing dose-dependent increase.

claim: Maintaining the iSAM iPSCs in the presence of SB fully restored the inducibility of the transgene with virtually all cells expressing mCherry in the presence of DOX.
source: We, therefore, maintained the iSAM iPSCs in the presence of SB and this fully restored the inducibility of the transgene with virtually all cells expressing mCherry in the presence of DOX (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing restored expression.

claim: Robust expression of the iSAM cassette was detected during the differentiation without SB treatment.
source: We did not treat the cells with SB during the differentiation since we detected robust expression of the iSAM cassette during the differentiation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data showing mCherry expression during differentiation.

claim: HDACs are involved in the chromatin remodelling during the EHT process.
source: Furthermore, since the HDACs are also involved in the chromatin remodelling during the EHT process (Thambyrajah et al., 2018), we predicted that SB treatment would negatively affect the differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The level of expression of the mCherry tag was proportional to the concentration of DOX in the RUNX1C-GFP hESC reporter cell line.
source: As predicted, the level of expression of the mCherry tag, the fluorescent mCherry reporter tag within the iSAM cassette, was proportional to the concentration of DOX (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E)
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing dose-response relationship.

claim: The number of cells in which RUNX1C-GFP was activated correlated with the concentration of DOX.
source: As predicted, the level of expression of the mCherry tag, the fluorescent mCherry reporter tag within the iSAM cassette, was proportional to the concentration of DOX (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E) and to the number of cells in which RUNX1C-GFP was activated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing correlation.

claim: The RUNX1C expression level, measured by the mean fluorescence intensity of the RUNX1C-GFP reporter, correlated with the concentration of DOX.
source: Furthermore, the RUNX1C expression level, measured by the mean fluorescence intensity of the RUNX1C-GFP reporter, also correlated with the concentration of DOX (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The manuscript presents flow cytometry data showing correlation.

claim: Only when iPSCs were transfected with both iSAM and the gRNA directed to RUNX1C and treated with DOX, was the expression of the RUNX1C gene and RUNX1 protein detected.
source: We then tested the iSAM cassette in the iPSC line (SFCi55) (Figure 2B–D). Only when iPSCs were transfected with both iSAM and the gRNA directed to RUNX1C and treated with DOX, was the expression of the RUNX1C gene and RUNX1 protein detected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR and immunostaining data showing specific activation.

claim: The iSAM strategy could activate RUNX1C expression in HeLa cells and this was correlated with the DOX concentration in a linear manner.
source: We demonstrated this strategy could activate RUNX1C expression in HeLa cells and that this was correlated with the DOX concentration in a linear manner (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The manuscript presents qPCR data showing linear dose-response relationship.
